runs.text: O ranger os dentes apertandoos cõ

lines.note: `Faguiximi` describes grinding the teeth in anger, not merely chewing. Portuguese `ranger os dentes` supplies the action; the cause continues below.
`ira` completes “clenching them in anger.” `Faguiximiuo ſuru` makes the preceding noun into an action with `suru`; read across the physical break.
`Faguqi` gives ハグキ. The first gloss is transcribed `Linguas`, which is lexically surprising for modern 歯茎; do not silently replace the Portuguese. The second sense concerns feathers.
This finishes `paſ- / ſaros`, “birds,” in the second sense of `Faguqi`. It is not a separate Japanese entry or a continuation of the next verb.
`Faguracaxi` introduces a causative-looking stem. Here `ir à mão` means checking or restraining someone; the definition continues with rebuke, not literal walking.

runs.text: der a alguem que eſta pera dizer, ou fazer al-

lines.note: The person is about to say or do something unsuitable. This supplies the human object of the restraint described above.

runs.text: gũa couſa que não conuem, com que fique como

lines.note: `que não conuem` qualifies the proposed action as inappropriate. The result clause begins `com que fique`, continued by embarrassment below.
`corrido` here means abashed, paired with `enuergonhado`, not “having run.” `Vmauo fa-` begins a separate horse example.

runs.text: Impedir o caualo que não faça, ou

lines.note: Join `fa- / guracaſu`: ウマヲ ハグラカス. The Portuguese now describes preventing the horse from performing an undesirable movement.

runs.text: ſaya com algũa manha, ou mouimento ruim

lines.note: `manha` denotes a trick or bad habit in this horse context. The clause continues the prevention, not a new sense of the headword.
Tightening the bridle is the means of restraint. `freo` is the historical Portuguese form corresponding to modern `freio`.
`Fagure` is explained here as becoming abashed or embarrassed. Modern はぐれる alone would not capture the specific social sense given in Portuguese.
`Mairi fagurete iyeni maira-` describes failing to make a visit through embarrassment; the final negative belongs to the next line.

runs.text: Não vir a viſitar a alguem com vergo-

lines.note: `maira- / nu` is the negative verb, “does not visit.” The Portuguese explains the absence as shame, completed below.

runs.text: nha por ter tardado, & não vir a tempo.

lines.note: The embarrassment results from having delayed and missed the proper time. This causal detail matters to the preceding Japanese example.
This `Fai` is 拝, with `Vogamu` オガム as its explanation. The Portuguese explicitly limits its grammatical use in the next line.

runs.text: ſe vſa ſenão com, xi, ſuru. Vt,

lines.note: `xi, ſuru` are Japanese verbal forms cited inside Portuguese prose. `Faiſu-` begins the actual example; the note is about inflection, not two Portuguese words.
`Faiſu- / ru` yields 拝する, “venerate or worship.” The short line completes both the Japanese example and its Portuguese gloss.
`Faino zǒ` means the lung organ; Portuguese `Bofes` confirms 肺. This is a different homograph from the preceding 拝.
Portuguese describes tender roots of a water-lily-like plant (`golfão`). Do not infer the exact plant or Japanese kanji solely from the spelling `Fai`.
`Cinza` means ash, identifying this `Fai` as 灰. It must remain separate from the neighboring homographs.
`Moſcas` means flies. The reading ハイ represents a historical form for the insect; changing it to modern ハエ would alter the source.
This verbal `Fai` means crawling. The dictionary's contracted inflectional forms `ǒ, ǒta` should not be mistaken for additional nouns.

runs.text: ro pello chão como os bichos, &c. ¶ Item,

lines.note: Crawling is compared to creatures moving close to the ground. `Item` begins an additional botanical application on the following line.

runs.text: Trepar, ou dilatarſe a era, ou outra erua ſeme-

lines.note: Here `era` is ivy, not the Portuguese past-tense verb. Creeping or spreading plants extend the bodily sense of はう.
This completes `ſeme- / lhante`, “similar,” qualifying other plants like ivy. No independent lexical material begins here.
`Fai aruqi` is crawling along, combining はい with 歩き. The Portuguese again specifies movement close to the ground.
`pollo chão` completes the preceding definition, “along the ground.” Its spelling is preserved rather than modernized to `pelo`.

runs.text: Hũa taboinha ſobre que poem o copo.

lines.note: `Faiban` denotes a small board on which a cup is placed, compatible with a cup stand or tray. The following entry has another sense of the same spelling.
The scan supports `Faiban`, not `Faibun`. `Rǒjeqi` ロウゼキ and Portuguese disorder describe the disarray of a drinking gathering; the later `Faibun` is distribution.

runs.text: bação que fica no Zaxiqi, depois de muito

lines.note: The disorder remains in the `Zaxiqi`, 座敷. That Japanese room name is embedded in the Portuguese definition, not an example sentence.
`beber` completes “after much drinking.” It explains the circumstances of the disorder rather than adding a new action to the Japanese entry.
This `Faibun` is 配分: `Cubari, vaquru` supplies distributing and dividing. Portuguese `Repartição` confirms the contrast with `Faiban` above.
`Faibuqi` is a grade of good silver, compatible with 灰吹 silver. The definition gives quality but does not itself describe the refining process.
`Faicacari` describes a child crawling toward someone. The following line supplies the parent as destination.

runs.text: pera o pay, ou mãy, &c. ¶ Item, Subir

lines.note: The child approaches father or mother. `Item` then introduces the parallel action of a climbing plant, not another child example.

runs.text: a era, ou outra erua ſemelhante polla aruore,

lines.note: Ivy or a similar plant climbs a tree. This is a botanical extension of the preceding crawling verb.
`ſebe` adds a hedge to the possible supports for the climbing plant. The short line closes that definition.

runs.text: Certo genero de verſos, ou cantigas im-

lines.note: `Faicai` is 俳諧. The Portuguese categorizes it as a kind of verse or song; its evaluative description continues below.

runs.text: perfeitas que hum faz, ou muitos juntos, vſan-

lines.note: The verses may be made by one person or collaboratively. `imperfeitas` is the compiler's characterization, not a claim that the transcription is incomplete.

runs.text: do de palauras ordinarias, & pouco polidas.

lines.note: Ordinary, unpolished words characterize the verse style in this definition. This supports the haikai identification without imposing a modern genre definition.
`Sacazzuqino vchi` is サカヅキノ ウチ, “inside the cup,” explaining `Faichǔ` 杯中. The Portuguese agrees directly.
`ou taça` adds another Portuguese word for a cup or bowl. It completes the preceding spatial definition.
`Yaburetaru cuni`, “a ruined country,” identifies `Faicocu` as a devastated realm. Keep the historical attributive `-taru` in the interpretation.

runs.text: Armas que cobrem as pernas de cima

lines.note: `Faidate` refers to armor covering the upper legs. The Portuguese definition locates it anatomically rather than merely calling it clothing.
The protection extends to the knees, completing the preceding armor definition. This fits the thigh-protection sense of はいだて.
`Faide, zzuru, eta` describes crawling out. The ending belongs to the historical 出づ series; `zzuru` is not an independent lexical headword.
`Faiden` is 拝殿, explained as `Vogamijo`, a place of worship. Its position relative to the shrine is specified below.
The oratory stands before the house of the `Cami`, the deity. This is a Japanese religious term embedded in Portuguese prose.
`Vogami yomu` means reading reverently, explaining 拝読. The two Japanese verbs and Portuguese `Ler com reuerẽcia` agree.
This `Faje` ハゼ denotes a fish. The sparse definition does not justify identifying a narrower species.

runs.text: Eſteiras feitas de hũa certa erua, ou

lines.note: A second `Faje` denotes mats made from a particular plant. Do not merge it with the fish entry despite identical spelling.

runs.text: palha groſſa pera dependurar das portas, va-

lines.note: The mats use coarse straw and are hung at doorways. The final `va-` continues as verandas below.
`va- / randas` completes the list of places where the mats hang. The line belongs to the material-object definition.
This `Faje` is parched or popped rice. Portuguese `torrado, & arrebentado` supports the bursting/popping sense of はぜ.
`Momi fajeni natta` means the rice has become popped rice. The predicate `ni natta` is the change-of-state construction.

runs.text: arrebentado, ou com o âmago ſaido pera fora.

lines.note: The Portuguese explains that the interior of the grain has emerged. This describes popping, not germination or ordinary cooking.
`Fai, l, fainoqi` gives a tree name and “fai tree.” Its wood is identified by the uses listed in the next two lines.

runs.text: os Faxis com que comem em Iapão, & que

lines.note: The wood makes `Faxis`, eating chopsticks. The Japanese pluralized term belongs inside the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: metem entre as duas canas do arco.

lines.note: It is also inserted between the two bamboo members of a bow. This second use is important botanical context but does not prove a species identification.
`Vogami firaqu` means respectfully opening, with `Faiqen` as a related expression. The Portuguese narrows this to reading letters reverently.
`car- / tas` completes “letters.” Respectful reading supplies the sense of the preceding 拝披-related entry.

runs.text: Faifocu. Yabure niguru. i, Gunginga cuz-

lines.note: `Yabure niguru` describes defeat and flight. `Gunginga` can be parsed as 軍陣が, with historical `gi` in the voiced palatal series; the army gloss below supports that reading without a spelling correction.
Join `cuz- / zururu` as 崩るる. The Portuguese states that the army is broken and flees, supporting the defeat sense of `Faifocu`.

runs.text: Prouiſão que ſe daa, ou paſſa pera ti-

lines.note: `Faifu` is an authorization or written order. The purpose begins with collecting something in the following line.

runs.text: rar algũa finta, ou fazer pagar algũa couſa.

lines.note: `finta` is a levy or assessment here. The document authorizes collecting a levy or making a payment, not merely distributing ordinary correspondence.
`Faifuuo iruru` illustrates issuing or delivering this authorization. The Portuguese `pro-` continues as `provisão` below.

runs.text: uiſão, ou papel pera eſte effeito.

lines.note: The paper is given for the stated fiscal purpose. This finishes the example and confirms the documentary sense of `Faifu`.

runs.text: Ir ao paço do Rei em certo tempo de feſ-

lines.note: This `Faiga` describes going to the king's palace at a festive time. It is a ceremonial visit, not simply private rejoicing.
`viſitalo` specifies visiting the ruler. The short line completes the first `Faiga` definition.
`Vogami yorocobu` combines reverence with rejoicing, compatible with 拝賀. This second entry explains the action rather than the ceremonial occasion.
`a- / legrandoſe` completes rejoicing. It modifies the reverential action described in the preceding line.
`Sutaretaru gacumon` is neglected or abandoned learning, explaining `Faigacu` 廃学. The Portuguese continues with forgotten studies.
The studies have been forgotten and left aside. `Fai-` begins the verbal example continued below.
`Fai- / gacu ſuru` means allowing one's learning to lapse. Portuguese explains forgetting what one has learned.
`aprendido` closes that object clause. This line completes the loss-of-learning example, not a new entry.

runs.text: Faigan. Cambaxeuo vogamu. i, vǒ meni

lines.note: `Cambaxeuo vogamu` concerns reverently seeing a person's face. `vǒ meni cacaru` is the respectful meeting expression; segmentation should be read across the next line.
`cacaru` completes お目にかかる. Portuguese specifies seeing a noble person with reverence, supporting `Faigan` 拝顔.

runs.text: Faigun. Icuſa yabururu. i, Ginga cuzzu-

lines.note: `Icuſa yabururu` and `Ginga cuzzu-` describe an army or formation breaking. `Ginga` can be read 陣が here; do not confuse it with 銀河.
`cuzzu- / ruru` finishes “break down.” Portuguese `Deſtruirſe o exercito` confirms the military defeat sense.

`Faijen` is 配膳. Here `Ien` is written with consonantal I for J: `Ienuo cubaru` is ゼンヲ クバル, 膳を配る. The human-confirmed interpretation agrees with the Portuguese arrangement of meal trays; the printed I is a spelling variant, not a transcription error.
The Japanese tables or trays are arranged in order in the `Zaxiqi`. This supports 膳 in the preceding `Ienuo`; the historical I/J spelling remains unchanged in Level 1.
`Fai iri` combines crawling with entering. The gloss `Entrar de gatinhas` confirms that this is a movement verb, not a 拝 compound.
`Vogami tçucayuru` is serving respectfully, compatible with 拝事. Portuguese begins the definition as service performed for someone.
The recipient is an honored person, and the manner is reverent. This completes the social relationship expressed by the Japanese gloss.
`Vogami, tatematçuru` explains a respectful offering. `Faijǒ` is in the series of honorific 拝 compounds, not the crawling family.

runs.text: dar a peſſoa nobre algũa couſa.

lines.note: The offering is something given to a noble person. Portuguese supplies the recipient and object absent from the short Japanese gloss.
`Vogami vquru` means receiving reverently, explaining 拝受. The movement of the gift is opposite to the preceding offering entry.

runs.text: ſa de peſſoa honrada com reuerencia.

lines.note: Something is received from an honored person with reverence. Read this as completion of the receiving definition.
`Faimauari` means crawling around. Its literal bodily sense is extended to climbing plants in the next line.

runs.text: nhas, ou ir trepãdo a era polla aruore em roda.

lines.note: The ivy winds around a tree. The Portuguese uses the same circular motion to connect the human and botanical applications.
`Aliquando, Permet.` marks an occasional metaphorical sense. The action becomes following someone persistently, continued below.

runs.text: guem com liſonjas pera auer algũa couſa delle.

lines.note: The follower uses flattery to obtain something. This is a social metaphor of crawling around someone, not another description of ivy.

`Faimǒ` introduces forgetful confusion; the Portuguese definition continues onto f166. `Xinnenxi` is linguistically uncertain here: do not invent a segmentation or kanji merely from the generated reading.
